The last room we show is the one we would have started with.

Five tall windows down one side, a floor that takes any weight, and enough distance from the entrance that a hundred people can arrive before the room knows it. It has no kitchen either. None of them do.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number nine.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Dinners in Tuscan villas, cloisters and historic houses with no kitchen of their own.

Six twenty in the morning, and nothing has been cooked yet.

Everything you see was carried in. Induction, 32 kW, through a door 1.10 m wide, which is the number that decides what is on the menu more often than the menu does.

Two hours to build. Gone by morning, and the floor from 1490 unmarked.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We build a full kitchen where there is none, and take it out again the same night.

The same room, sixty covers, one table.

Sixty at a single table is a decision and not a constraint: two tables of thirty are easier to serve, and they make two parties instead of one. So the table runs the length of the room, the brigade works from both ends inward, and the last plate goes down within four minutes of the first.

There is no kitchen in this building. There never was.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number nine, at night.

A loggia is half a room, and the missing half decides everything.

No wall on the garden side means no power on that side either, so the service line runs along the wall behind and the field kitchen goes out of sight in the courtyard. Forty covers along the length, one row, never two.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number ten.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We open rooms that are not for hire, for one evening, and put them back as we found them.

A board is not a large plate.

It is composed to be taken apart: everything has to be lifted without moving anything else, and the last person to arrive has to find it still legible. So it is built in sectors rather than in a heap, and the cheeses sit on the opposite side from where the wine is poured.

After ten minutes it becomes a different object. That one has to stand up too.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Fifty covers out of a field kitchen, in houses that have none.

A room built to hold wine, not people. Brick vaults, two empty vats, and a stone channel in the floor that still runs the right way.

No kitchen, no power beyond one bare bulb, and a door that takes the trolley only if you take the wheels off first.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eleven.

Three glasses per place, and two of them will not be used.

They go down anyway, because the third one is for whatever gets opened after the second course, and a table you have to add to halfway through has already lost the evening.

The napkin is bordeaux. That part is not practical.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Brigade, field kitchen and service, carried into rooms that have neither.

The same vat room, between the two vats.

Twenty covers in a room built for wine and not for people: brick vaults, a drainage channel in the floor and one bare bulb. Everything you can see arrived from outside, and the door takes the trolley only if you take the wheels off first.

Rooms like this are on nobody's price list.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eleven, at night.

Halfway through, a table stops looking laid and starts looking used.

This is the state we work towards rather than away from: bread broken where somebody reached for it, glasses at different levels, a napkin left on a chair. A table that still looks photographed at ten o'clock is a table where nobody has relaxed.

We clear the plates. We leave the rest alone.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners for twelve to a hundred, in rooms that are not venues.

A villa with a kitchen is still a villa without a kitchen.

The one that is there is domestic: two burners, one oven, one sink, and a fridge that runs at eight degrees instead of four. It is somewhere to set down and somewhere to wash, not somewhere to cook for fifty. The field kitchen comes anyway, and this room becomes the place where the plates go out.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twelve.

A larder that travels is counted in crates, not in shelves.

The night before it is all inside, weighed, and no crate goes over twenty-five kilos, because one person has to carry it up a staircase with no lift. That constraint is what decides how many jars, and how much glass.

Glass always loses. It gets decanted.

A cellar is the only room in the dossier that does not change temperature.

It sits between twelve and fourteen degrees all year, which is perfect for the wine and wrong for everything else: the plates are heated elsewhere and arrive covered, and the bread is cut at the last minute because down here it dries in twenty minutes.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number thirteen.

Meat rests almost as long as it cooked.

Straight from the fire to the board and the liquid ends up on the table instead of in the plate. Twenty minutes somewhere warm does not cool it down: it makes it carvable. The plate underneath, on the other hand, has to be hot enough to hurt.

It is the only moment in the service when the right thing to do is wait.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Seasonal Tuscan cooking, plated where there is no kitchen.

The same cellar, at twelve degrees all year round.

Perfect for the wine and wrong for everything else. The plates are heated two rooms away and carried covered, and the bread is cut at the last minute because down here it dries in twenty minutes. The vault takes the sound and gives nothing back, so eighteen people at one table sound like eight.

Nobody advertises a room like this. You have to know that it exists.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number thirteen, at night.
